#### Bulk gravity perspective:

As discussed in section 2.1, the system has a bulk description in terms of gravity on an asymptotically AdSd+1 spacetime containing a codimension-one brane, which splits the bulk into two halves – see figure 3a. The brane is characterized by the tension $T_{o}$ and also the DGP coupling $1/G_{\textrm{\tiny brane}}$ , introduced in eqs. (5) and (49), respectively. We can use the Israel junction conditions (10) to determine the location of the brane as embedded in the higher dimensional space. The backreaction causes warping around the brane, and after a change of coordinates, tuning the brane tension can be understood as moving the brane further into a new asymptotic AdS region, as seen in eq. (12) or (13). For large brane tension, i.e., with $\varepsilon\ll 1$ , the spectrum of graviton fluctuations in the bulk is almost unchanged with respect to the modes in empty AdS space. However, a new set of graviton states also appear localized at the brane [43, 42], as illustrated figure 4. These are created by the nonlinear coupling of gravity to the brane. Unlike in the Randall-Sundrum model with a flat or de Sitter brane, the new graviton modes are not actually massless on the brane, but merely very light states whose wavefunction peaks around the brane [44, 61]. The remaining bulk graviton modes appear as a tower of Kaluza-Klein states, from the point of view of the theory on the brane, with masses of ${\cal O}(1/\ell_{\textrm{\tiny eff}})$ set by the curvature scale of the $d$ -dimensional AdS geometry on the brane. These results have been studied in quite some detail [44, 61, 80, 81, 82, 62] for Randall-Sundrum branes, but it is interesting to examine how the spectrum is modified by the DGP term (49). We will make some qualitative statements about this question below, but leave a detailed quantitative discussion and the interpretation of this mechanism from the point of view of the CFT for future work [77].

#### Brane perspective:

This second perspective, discussed in section 2.2, effectively integrates out the spatial direction between the asymptotically AdS boundary and the brane to produce an effective action (23) for Randall-Sundrum/DGP gravity on the brane, with the new localized graviton state playing the role of the $d$ -dimensional graviton. Hence, we are left with a $d$ -dimensional theory of gravity coupled to (two copies of) the dual CFT on the brane – see figure 3b. As discussed in the description of the bulk perspective, amongst the new localized bulk modes, we have an almost massless graviton but also a tower of massive Kaluza-Klein states with masses of ${\cal O}(1/\ell_{\textrm{\tiny eff}})$ . In section 2.2, we demonstrated the consistency between the bulk gravity perspective and the brane perspective by observing how the equations of motion of the new effective action fix the brane position in the ambient spacetime. Of course, the bulk physics is also dual to the dual CFT on the asymptotic AdSd+1 boundary, and so this description is completed by coupling the gravitational and CFT degrees of freedom on the brane to the CFT on the fixed boundary geometry. We refer to that latter as the bath CFT. Next, we discuss how different parameters in the brane perspective are related to bulk parameters.

There are four independent parameters which characterize the gravitational theory on the brane: the curvature scale $\ell_{\textrm{\tiny eff}}$ , the effective Newton’s constant $G_{\textrm{\tiny eff}}$ , the central charge of the boundary CFT $c_{\textrm{\tiny T}}$ , and the effective short-distance cutoff $\tilde{\delta}$ . These emerge from the bulk theory through the four parameters characterizing the latter: the bulk curvature scale $L$ , the bulk Newton’s constant $G_{\textrm{\tiny bulk}}$ , the brane Newton’s constant $G_{\textrm{\tiny brane}}$ and the brane tension $T_{o}$ .1515 15 Recall that $\Delta T$ is determined by these parameters in eq. (51), as well as eqs. (12) and (16). From eq. (24), we see that $\ell_{\textrm{\tiny eff}}$ is determined by a specific combination of $T_{o}$ , $G_{\textrm{\tiny bulk}}$ and $L$ . Similarly, $G_{\textrm{\tiny eff}}$ is determined by $G_{\textrm{\tiny brane}}$ , $G_{\textrm{\tiny bulk}}$ and $L$ in eq. (52). The central charge of the boundary CFT is given by the standard expression $c_{\textrm{\tiny T}}\sim L^{d-1}/G_{\textrm{\tiny bulk}}$ , e.g., see [83].

Lastly, as discussed in section 2.2, the theory on the brane comes with a short-distance cutoff $\tilde{\delta}$ [56, 63, 64] at which the description of the brane theory in terms of (two copies of) the boundary CFT coupled to Einstein gravity breaks down. Following a standard bulk analysis, one would see that correlators of local operators (with appropriate gravitational dressings) now longer exhibit the expected CFT behaviour at short distances of order

$$ \tilde{\delta}_{\textrm{\tiny CFT}}\sim L\,. $$

We denote this cutoff with the subscript ‘CFT’ to emphasize that the description of the matter degrees of freedom on the brane as a local $d$ -dimensional CFT is failing at distances smaller than this short-distance cutoff. However, we stress that there is another scale $\tilde{\delta}_{\textrm{\tiny GR}}$ , which is the distance at which the approximation of Einstein gravity on the brane breaks down. The simple parameter counting above shows that this cannot be an independent scale. For the brane perspective, the true cutoff $\tilde{\delta}$ where the description in terms of the dual CFT coupled to Einstein gravity fails is

$$ \tilde{\delta}={\rm max}\left\{\tilde{\delta}_{\textrm{\tiny CFT}}\,,\ \tilde{\delta}_{\textrm{\tiny GR}}\right\}\,. $$

We now discuss how $\tilde{\delta}_{\textrm{\tiny GR}}$ is related to the other scales in the brane theory.

Recall that integrating out the bulk degrees of freedom produces a series of higher curvature terms in the effective action (23), and hence demanding that $d$ -dimensional Einstein gravity provides a good approximation of the brane theory introduces constraints. The suppression of these higher curvature corrections requires that the ratio $L/\ell_{\textrm{\tiny eff}}$ be small. However, if we examine eq. (23) carefully and note the distinction $G_{\textrm{\tiny eff}}\neq G_{\textrm{\tiny RS}}$ , then suppressing the curvature-squared terms requires that

$$ \frac{1}{1+\lambda_{b}}\,\frac{L^{2}}{\ell_{\textrm{\tiny eff}}^{2}}\ll 1\,, $$

using eq. (54). Note that for fixed bulk and boundary curvature scales, this implies a lower bound on the DGP term, such that $\lambda_{b}$ cannot be arbitrarily close to $-1$ . For a pure RS brane with no additional DGP gravity, i.e., $\lambda_{b}=0$ , we conclude that the cutoff below which we find Einstein gravity coincides with the CFT cutoff $\tilde{\delta}_{\textrm{\tiny GR}}\sim\tilde{\delta}_{\textrm{\tiny CFT}}\sim L$ . More generally then, the above expression suggests that the DGP term (49) affects a shift producing a new short-distance cutoff for gravity,

$$ \tilde{\delta}_{\textrm{\tiny GR}}\sim\frac{L}{\sqrt{1+\lambda_{b}}}\ \sim\frac{\tilde{\delta}_{\textrm{\tiny CFT}}}{\sqrt{1+\lambda_{b}}}\,. $$

Hence the true cutoff (56) depends on the sign of $\lambda_{b}$ – we return to this point below. We should note that this result only applies for $d>4$ . For $d=4$ , the coefficient of the curvature-squared term is logarithmic in the cutoff, while for $d=2$ or $3$ , this interaction is not associated with a UV divergence.

While the above are UV effects, there are also IR effects resulting from having a large number of matter degrees of freedom propagating on the brane, as explained in [84, 85, 86]. The usual regime of validity for QFT in semiclassical gravity lies at energy scales below the Planck mass, or at distance scales larger than $G_{\textrm{\tiny eff}}^{1/(d-2)}$ . However, the boundary CFT has a large number of degrees of freedom, as indicated by the large $c_{\textrm{\tiny T}}$ , and hence the semiclassical description of gravity in fact breaks down much earlier. A direct way to see this breakdown [85] is to consider the computation of the (canonically normalized) graviton two-point function. In the high energy approximation, i.e., ignoring the AdS geometry, we have here:1616 16 This propagator argument can also be applied for the higher curvature terms discussed above. For example, the curvature-squared terms gives a perturbative correction: $\langle h(p)\,h(-p)\rangle\sim p^{-2}\left[1+\frac{L^{2}}{1+\lambda_{b}}\,p^{2}+\cdots\right]$ . Hence this approach yields the same result for the cutoff in eq. (58).

$$ \langle h(p)\,h(-p)\rangle\sim p^{-2}\left[1+c_{\textrm{\tiny T}}\,G_{\textrm{\tiny eff}}\,p^{d-2}+\cdots\right]\,. $$

The leading correction arises from a diagram involving the external gravitons coupling to the CFT stress tensor two-point function. We see that such corrections are only suppressed relative to the ‘tree-level’ result for momenta below a cutoff scale of order $(c_{\textrm{\tiny T}}G_{\textrm{\tiny eff}})^{-1/(d-2)}$ . For our model, the gravitational theory of the brane can therefore only be treated semiclassically for distance scales larger than

$$ \tilde{\delta}_{\textrm{\tiny GR}}\sim(c_{\textrm{\tiny T}}G_{\textrm{\tiny eff}})^{1/(d-2)}\sim\frac{L}{(1+\lambda_{b})^{1/(d-2)}}\sim\frac{\tilde{\delta}_{\textrm{\tiny CFT}}}{(1+\lambda_{b})^{1/(d-2)}}\,. $$

Again, for a pure RS brane with $\lambda_{b}=0$ , the cutoffs for Einstein gravity and the CFT agree, yielding $\tilde{\delta}\sim L$ . However, the addition of a DGP gravity term modifies the cutoff, but in a manner distinct from eq. (58), produced by the higher curvature terms. Note that the above result applies for $d\geq 3$ .

The distinction between these two cutoffs indicates that these are really two different physical phenomena contributing to the breakdown of Einstein gravity in the brane perspective. Note that $\lambda_{b}>0$ , in both eqs. (58) and (60), the effect is to produce a shorter cutoff scale, however, the second limit (60) is the first to contribute (where we are assuming $d>4$ ). However, this result is smaller that $\tilde{\delta}_{\textrm{\tiny CFT}}$ and hence from eq. (56), we find

$$ \lambda_{b}>0\ \ :\qquad\tilde{\delta}\sim\tilde{\delta}_{\textrm{\tiny CFT}}\sim L\,. $$

On the other hand with $\lambda_{b}<0$ , the cutoff $\tilde{\delta}_{\textrm{\tiny GR}}$ is pushed to larger distance scales. In this case, eq. (58) is the first to modify the gravitational physics on the brane as we move to smaller distances. Further since this result is now larger than the CFT cutoff, in this regime, eq. (56) yields

$$ \lambda_{b}<0\ \ :\qquad\tilde{\delta}\sim\tilde{\delta}_{\textrm{\tiny GR}}\sim\frac{L}{\sqrt{1+\lambda_{b}}}\,. $$

Let us also note that the latter effect, i.e., CFT corrections to the graviton propagator, are also responsible for the mass of the brane graviton [80]. It is interesting to note that if we take the high energy limit of the corrections to the graviton propagator, eq. (59), we can estimate a mass correction for low energy gravitons mode of roughly

$$ \displaystyle\frac{c_{\textrm{\tiny T}}G_{\textrm{\tiny eff}}}{\ell_{\textrm{\tiny eff}}^{d}}\sim\frac{1}{(1+\lambda_{b})\,\ell_{\textrm{\tiny eff}}^{\,2}}\left(\frac{L}{\ell_{\textrm{\tiny eff}}}\right)^{d-2}, $$

where we have substituted the $d$ -dimensional AdS scale as a lower bound on the momentum. The scaling with the d-dimensional cosmological constant $-\frac{1}{\ell^{2}_{\text{eff}}}$ agrees with predictions in the Karch-Randall model [81, 82]. However, we caution the reader that the above argument by which we obtained the scaling is heuristic at best. Importantly, whether or not the graviton actually obtains a mass correction depends on the boundary conditions of the matter fields in AdS and can therefore not be determined by a local argument alone [80]. However, taking eq. (63) at face value, we also see that a negative DGP coupling increases the mass scale, and vice versa for a positive coupling. This can be confirmed explicitly from bulk calculations [77].

#### Boundary perspective:

As the preceding discussion has made clear, the theory obtained by integrating out the bulk between the asymptotic boundary and the brane, has an effective description of the brane in terms of a local $d$ -dimensional CFT coupled to Einstein gravity up to some cutoff (56). However, the standard rules of AdS/CFT also allow for a fully microscopic description of the system in terms of the boundary theory. This is obtained by integrating out the bulk – including the brane – and the result is given by the bath CFT on the fixed $d$ -dimensional boundary geometry coupled to a ( $d-1$ )-dimensional conformal defect (positioned where the brane reaches the asymptotic boundary, i.e., the equator of the boundary sphere) – see figure 3c.

The bath CFT is characterized by the central charge $c_{\textrm{\tiny T}}\sim L^{d-1}/G_{\textrm{\tiny bulk}}$ , while the defect is characterized by its defect central charge $\tilde{c}_{\textrm{\tiny T}}\sim\ell_{\textrm{\tiny eff}}^{d-2}/G_{\textrm{\tiny eff}}$ . We note that in the absence of a DGP term, increasing the brane tension increases the defect central charge $\tilde{c}_{\textrm{\tiny T}}$ . Further, we note that the ratio of these two charges is given by

$$ \frac{\tilde{c}_{\textrm{\tiny T}}}{c_{\textrm{\tiny T}}}\sim\left(\frac{\ell_{\textrm{\tiny eff}}}{L}\right)^{d-2}(1+\lambda_{b})\,. $$

Following the standard AdS/CFT dictionary, the ratio $\ell_{\textrm{\tiny eff}}/L$ also translates to a ratio of couplings in the defect and bath CFTs,1717 17 Remember that the AdS/CFT dictionary tells us that $G_{N}\sim\ell_{\textrm{\tiny AdS}}^{d-1}/N_{dof}$ and $\lambda_{\text{Hooft}}\sim(\ell_{\textrm{\tiny AdS}}/\ell_{\textrm{\tiny s}})^{d}$ .

$$ {\tilde{\lambda}}/{\lambda}\sim{\ell_{\textrm{\tiny eff}}}/{L}\,. $$

Since we do not have a particular string construction in mind here, $\lambda$ should be thought of some positive power of the ‘t Hooft coupling of the bath CFT, while $\tilde{\lambda}$ will be some (different) positive power of the analogous coupling for the defect CFT.

Now the parameters in this boundary description must be constrained if we want to be in the regime where the brane perspective is valid. In particular, the latter requires that the brane curvature scale must be much larger than the effective cutoff, i.e.,

$$ \ell_{\textrm{\tiny eff}}/\tilde{\delta}\gg 1\,. $$

Now as described above, the cutoff has a separate form depending on whether $\lambda_{b}$ is positive or negative. Eq. (61) applies for $\lambda_{b}>0$ , which then yields $\ell_{\textrm{\tiny eff}}/L\gg 1$ . Hence we must have ${\tilde{\lambda}}/{\lambda}\gg 1$ and also $\tilde{c}_{\textrm{\tiny T}}/c_{\textrm{\tiny T}}\gg 1$ since $1+\lambda_{b}>1$ in this case. Similarly for $\lambda_{b}<0$ , combining eqs. (62) and (66) yields $\ell_{\textrm{\tiny eff}}/L\gg 1/\sqrt{1+\lambda_{b}}$ . In this case, $1+\lambda_{b}<1$ and it is straightforward to again show that the ratios must be constrained in the same manner. Hence for either sign of $\lambda_{b}$ , we have

$$ {\tilde{\lambda}}/{\lambda}\gg 1\qquad{\rm and}\qquad\tilde{c}_{\textrm{\tiny T}}/c_{\textrm{\tiny T}}\gg 1\,. $$

The large ratio of the central charges can also be heuristically understood requiring that energy and information are only leaking very slowly from the dynamical gravity region into the bath [28]. It has been argued that this ratio also sets the Page time [28]. With the boundary perspective, this can be understood as a requirement which ensures that the degrees of freedom on the defect and the CFT only slowly mix.

Lastly, the $d$ -dimensional graviton can be understood as a field dual to the lightest operator appearing in the boundary OPE expansion of the CFT stress energy tensor [87]. At weak coupling, one would naively assume that the lightest operator has dimension $\Delta=d$ . However, due to strong coupling effects it becomes possible that a negative anomalous dimension of roughly $-1$ is obtained, so that the corresponding operator can act as the holographic dual to a $d$ -dimensional graviton. The mass of the lightest state then signals that the anomalous dimension is not quite $-1$ , such that the dimension of the boundary operator dual to the graviton is $\Delta\geq d-1$ .

## 4 Holographic EE on the Brane

In this section, we shall look for ‘quantum extremal islands’ using the holographic setup described in the previous sections. Of course, quantum extremal islands have recently proven especially enlightening in the context of the black hole information paradox in two-dimensional JT gravity, where the emergence of these islands has signalled a transition to a phase where entropy of the Hawking radiation decreases over time, e.g., [20, 22, 23, 29, 26, 25, 73]. Some preliminary investigations of quantum extremal islands in higher dimensions also appeared in [21, 24]. In a companion paper [47], we will use the holographic model developed here to further extend these discussions to consider the black holes in arbitrary dimensions. However, in our present discussion black holes are not involved. Rather, we are simply considering the holographic entanglement entropies for certain regions in the vacuum of the boundary CFT coupled to the conformal defect. In situations to be discussed below, we find that the corresponding RT surfaces cross the brane in the bulk and this can be interpreted in terms of the appearance of a quantum extremal island in the effective theory of gravity on the brane.

In section 4.1 we will describe the regions we are considering and the possible RT surfaces. Section 4.2 discusses the extremization procedure of the RT surface in the presence of a brane and derives the conditions an RT surface needs to obey in our setting. Further, section 4.3 shows that the leading contribution of the RT surface close to the brane can be understood as the Dong-Wald entropy on the brane, as seen from the brane perspective. In section 4.4 we show an explicit calculation in $d=3$ and investigate the choices of parameters necessary to obtain quantum extremal islands. In particular, there, we will consider adding a DGP coupling to the bulk theory.

### 4.1 Holographic setup

*Figure 5: A timeslice of our CFT setup. A conformal defect running along the equator separates the two halves of R and its corresponding engangling surface $\Sigma_{\textrm{\tiny CFT}}$ .*

In the remainder of this chaper, we will focus on a specific calculation of the entanglement entropy (EE): We consider the vacuum state of our boundary CFT on $\mathbb{R}(\text{time})\times S^{d-1}(\text{space})$ with a conformal defect running along the equator of the $S^{d-1}$ . As described in section 2, the bulk spacetime has locally an AdSd+1 geometry and is bisected by a brane extending out to the defect position on the asymptotic boundary. Now we wish to evaluate the EE in the boundary CFT for a region $\mathbf{R}$ comprised of the union of two polar spherical caps on the $S^{d-1}$ – see figure 5. We follow the usual holographic prescription to compute the EE. That is, we examine the bulk surfaces $\mathbf{V}$ which are homologous to $\mathbf{R}$ and extremize the generalized entropy functional

$$ S_{\textrm{\tiny EE}}(\mathbf{R})={\rm min}\left\{{\rm ext}\,S_{\textrm{\tiny gen}}(\mathbf{V})\right\}={\rm min}\left\{{\rm ext}\left(\frac{A(\mathbf{V})}{4G_{\textrm{\tiny bulk}}}+\frac{A(\mathbf{V}\cap{\rm brane})}{4G_{\textrm{\tiny brane}}}\right)\right\}\,. $$

Of course, the first term above corresponds to the usual Ryu-Takayanagi (RT) term [7, 6] while, as discussed in appendix A, we expect the second term to arise whenever the bulk surface crosses a DGP brane.1818 18 Implicitly, eq. (68) assumes that the bulk and brane gravitational actions both correspond to the Einstein-Hilbert action (with a cosmological constant term), as in eqs. (4) and (49). Let us denote the extremal bulk surface as $\Sigma_{\mathbf{R}}$ , and the intersection with the brane $\sigma_{\mathbf{R}}=\Sigma_{\mathbf{R}}\cap{\rm brane}$ , see figure 7. Importantly, if there are multiple extrema, the EE is given by chosing the extremal surface yielding the smallest value for $S_{\textrm{\tiny gen}}(\Sigma_{\mathbf{R}})$ , as indicated above.

For the calculation described above, the candidate RT surfaces are anchored at the AdS boundary to the entangling surface $\Sigma_{\textrm{\tiny CFT}}=\partial\mathbf{R}=\partial\Sigma_{\mathbf{R}}$ , i.e., the boundaries of these surfaces are comprised of two $(d-2)$ -spheres, which are the boundaries of the two polar caps. We will find that there are two topologically distinct candidates for $\Sigma_{\mathbf{R}}$ which extremize the generalized entropy in eq. (68), see figure 8. The first consists of two disconnected disks on either side of the brane (in which case $\sigma_{\mathbf{R}}=\{\varnothing\}$ ). The second candidate has a cylindrical geometry which pierces the brane. Hence it is only in this latter case that the second term contributes in eq. (68). As noted above, the correct RT surface is chosen from these two candidates as the one which yields a smaller generalized entropy. Generally, we shall find that when the two polar caps are small, the disconnected discs are favoured, while the cylindrical surface can be the leading saddle for when the polar caps are large. We will denote the first situation as the ‘disconnected’ phase and the latter as the ‘connected’ phase. As we will describe in section 4.4, the details of the transition between these two phases also depends on other parameters in the holographic model, e.g., the tension and gravitational coupling of the brane.

To understand the interpretation of these results in terms of quantum extremal islands, we turn to the ‘brane perspective’ described in the previous section. This effective description gives the ‘island rule’ proposed in [22] for the entanglement entropy,

$$ \displaystyle S_{\textrm{\tiny EE}}(\mathbf{R}) \displaystyle= \displaystyle{\rm min}\left\{{\rm ext}\,S_{\textrm{\tiny gen}}(R\cup\text{islands})\right\} \displaystyle= \displaystyle{\rm min}\left\{{\rm ext}\left(S_{\textrm{\tiny EE}}(R\cup\text{islands})+\frac{A\left(\partial(\mathrm{islands})\right)}{4G_{\textrm{\tiny brane}}}\right)\right\}\,. $$

As geometries $\mathbf{R}=R$ , but we have used a different font on the right-hand side to emphasize the fact that the effective ‘brane perspective’ does not give the same detailed description of the CFT state on $\mathbf{R}$ , as the boundary or bulk perspectives. Based on our discussion in the previous sections, one might have expected that the gravitational term in eq. (69) would involve $G_{\textrm{\tiny eff}}$ rather than $G_{\textrm{\tiny brane}}$ . This is implicit in (69), as we will see below. In the presence of an island, the first term $S_{\textrm{\tiny EE}}(R\cup\text{islands})$ receives two large contributions, coming from the asymptotic AdS boundary and the region close to the brane. It is this second term, proportional to $1/G_{\text{RS}}$ , which combines with the last term in eq. (69) to yield the expected island contribution proportional to $1/G_{\textrm{\tiny eff}}$ , c.f. eq. (52).

It is now straightforward to interpret the previous holographic discussion in terms of the effective theory on the brane, eq. (69). In the connected phase, the holographic RT surface crosses the brane and (if DGP couplings are turned on) we see an explicit brane contribution in eq. (68). From the brane perspective, a quantum extremal island has formed in the gravitational region (i.e., the region on the brane enclosed by $\sigma_{\mathbf{R}}$ )1919 19 Let us add that from the bulk perspective, entanglement wedge reconstruction [88, 89, 90, 91, 92, 93, 94] ensures that operators within this island can be reconstructed from boundary CFT data in $\mathbf{R}$ . and the analogous gravitational term appears in the island rule (69). The bulk RT contribution in eq. (68) corresponds to $S_{\textrm{\tiny EE}}(R\cup\text{islands})$ in eq. (69). As alluded to above, this makes clear that the gravitational contribution to the island is comprised of two components: the bare contribution $\sim 1/G_{\textrm{\tiny brane}}$ , which arises from a DGP coupling added to the brane, and the bulk contribution proportional to $L/G_{\textrm{\tiny bulk}}$ , which arises from the volume of the RT surface close to the brane. To see how the latter arises in the effective theory, notice that we can split $S_{\textrm{\tiny EE}}$ into UV-finite and UV-‘divergent’ contributions close to the brane, where the latter are contributions proportional to inverse powers of $z_{\textrm{\tiny B}}$ . These are the analog of the UV divergent boundary contributions for the boundary CFT in the regions without gravity. As discussed in section 3, the brane position imposes a UV cutoff for the CFT on the brane, and hence the corresponding ‘divergent’ contributions to the EE are in fact finite and instead yield contributions which match those expected for the gravitational entropy from the induced contributions to eq. (23). This makes contact with the usual notion of generalized entropy as the sum of the geometric gravitational entropy and the entropy of the quantum fields [18, 19].

In the disconnected phase, the EE only involves the modes enclosed within the two polar caps and there is no contribution from the CFT in the gravitational region, i.e., on the AdSd brane. In passing, let us recall that the short wavelength modes in the vicinity of the entangling surface $\Sigma_{\textrm{\tiny CFT}}$ produce various UV divergent boundary contributions, such as the celebrated area law term [95, 96, 97]. Of course, in both phases these contributions are regulated in the holographic calculation by introducing a cutoff surface near the asymptotic AdS boundary [9].

### 4.2 RT meets the Brane

In this section, we shall introduce some technical details, which are useful to calculate the EE associated with the two polar caps in the boundary CFT. In particular, we examine the behaviour of the bulk RT surface $\Sigma_{\mathbf{R}}$ as it crosses the brane, i.e., how the intersection surface $\sigma_{\mathbf{R}}$ is determined. However, we begin by specifying our EE calculation more precisely and reviewing the metrics describing the bulk spacetime.

Let us describe the $\mathbb{R}\times S^{d-1}$ geometry on which the boundary CFT lives with,

$$ ds^{2}=R^{2}\left[-dt^{2}+d\theta^{2}+\sin^{2}\!\theta\,d\Omega_{d-2}^{2}\right]\,, $$

where $R$ is the radius of curvature of the $(d-1)$ -sphere. The polar angle $\theta$ runs over $0\leq\theta\leq\pi$ , and the conformal defect sits at the equator $\theta=\pi/2$ . As illustrated in figure 5, we wish to evaluate the EE in the boundary CFT for a region $\mathbf{R}$ comprised of two polar caps on the $S^{d-1}$ . More specifically, we choose the entangling surface $\Sigma_{\textrm{\tiny CFT}}$ to be two circles placed symmetrically on either side of the defect at $\theta=\pi/2\pm\theta_{\textrm{\tiny CFT}}$ . Hence we are evaluating the EE between these two balls and the complementary region, which corresponds to a ‘belt’ of width $2\theta_{\textrm{\tiny CFT}}$ centered on the conformal defect.

Turning now to the bulk geometry, recall that in section 2.1, we discussed the background solution in terms a metric where the AdSd+1 geometry was foliated by AdSd slices. Eq. (9) describes the local geometry on either side of the brane located at $z=z_{\textrm{\tiny B}}$ with

$$ ds^{2}=\frac{L^{2}}{z^{2}}\left[dz^{2}+L^{2}\left(1+\frac{z^{2}}{4\,L^{2}}\right)^{2}\left(-\cosh^{2}\!{\tilde{r}}\,dt^{2}+d{\tilde{r}}^{2}+\sinh^{2}\!{\tilde{r}}\,d\Omega_{d-2}^{2}\right)\right]\,. $$

While these coordinates are well suited to discuss the brane geometry, we also consider ‘global’ coordinates for the AdSd+1 geometry

$$ ds^{2}=L^{2}\left[-\cosh^{2}\!r\,dt^{2}+dr^{2}+\sinh^{2}\!r\,\left(d\theta^{2}+\sin^{2}\!\theta\,d\Omega_{d-2}^{2}\right)\right]\,, $$

which are better adapted to discuss the boundary theory. That is, up to a Weyl rescaling, the geometry on fixed $r$ surfaces matches eq. (70) in the asymptotic region, and the UV regulator surface needed to properly define the holographic EE can be simply chosen as some slice $r=r_{\textrm{\tiny UV}}\gg L$ .

However, while we refer to eq. (72) as ‘global’ coordinates, they do not cover the entire back-reacted bulk solution depicted in figure 2. Rather we use the coordinates in eq. (72) to cover two patches on either side of the brane and near the asymptotic AdSd+1 boundary.2020 20 Of course, the same applies for the previous coordinates in eq. (71). Comparing eqs. (71) and (72), it is straightforward to identify the transformation between the two coordinate systems as

$$ \tanh{\tilde{r}}=\tanh r\sin\theta\,,\quad\frac{z}{L}=-2\sinh r\,\cos\theta\pm 2\sqrt{\sinh^{2}\!r\,\cos^{2}\!\theta+1}\,. $$

With the + (–) sign, the brane at $z=z_{\textrm{\tiny B}}\ll L$ resides near the boundary hemisphere with $0\leq\theta\leq\pi/2$ ( $\pi/2\leq\theta\leq\pi$ ) and $r\to\infty$ . Therefore letting $\theta$ run from 0 to $\pi$ on the boundary with the defect at $\theta=\pi/2$ , we choose the – (+) sign to cover the patch covering the asymptotic boundary hemisphere $0\leq\theta\leq\pi/2$ ( $\pi/2\leq\theta\leq\pi$ ).

Using the AdS foliation (71), the position of the brane was specified by $z=z_{\textrm{\tiny B}}$ . In terms of the global coordinates (72) , the brane position can be specified with

$$ \sinh^{2}\!r\,\cos^{2}\!\theta=\frac{L^{2}}{z_{\textrm{\tiny B}}^{2}}\left(1-\frac{z_{\textrm{\tiny B}}^{2}}{4L^{2}}\right)^{2}\,. $$

The specific sign of $\cos\theta$ depends on whether one considers the coordinate patch above or below the brane – see comments below eq. (73). Further, we reach the asymptotic boundary on the brane by taking ${\tilde{r}}\to\infty$ , which in the global coordinates then corresponds to $r\to\infty$ and $\theta\to\pi/2$ . Hence, we see that the brane intersects the asymptotic boundary at the position of the conformal defect, as expected.

To examine the behaviour of the bulk RT surface $\Sigma_{\mathbf{R}}$ where it crosses the brane, it is useful to consider the problem of extremal surfaces using the metric (71). Because the bulk geometry is static, the RT surfaces will be confined to a constant time slice in the bulk. The entangling surfaces in the boundary are spherically symmetric and so we only need to consider bulk surfaces with the same rotational symmetry on the $S^{d-2}$ , that is, we parametrize the surfaces as ${\tilde{r}}={\tilde{r}}(z)$ and the bulk contribution to the holographic EE is then given by

$$ S_{\textrm{\tiny bulk}}=2\,\frac{L^{d-1}\,\Omega_{d-2}}{4\,G_{\textrm{\tiny bulk}}}\int\frac{dz}{z}\,\left[\frac{L}{z}\left(1+\frac{z^{2}}{4\,L^{2}}\right)\sinh{\tilde{r}}\right]^{d-2}\sqrt{1+L^{2}\left(1+\frac{z^{2}}{4\,L^{2}}\right)^{2}\left(\frac{d{\tilde{r}}}{dz}\right)^{2}} $$

where $\Omega_{d-2}$ is the area of a unit $(d-2)$ -sphere.2121 21 Recall that the area of a unit $n$ -sphere is given by $\Omega_{n}=2\pi^{\frac{n+1}{2}}/\Gamma\left(\frac{n+1}{2}\right)$ . An overall factor of 2 is included here because we assume that the profile ${\tilde{r}}(z)$ will be reflection symmetric about the brane, and hence $S_{\textrm{\tiny RT}}$ recieves the same contribution from both sides.

Treating eq. (75) as an action, we would derive an ‘Euler-Lagrange’ equation for the profile whose solution corresponds to an extremal surface in the bulk, i.e., away from the brane.2222 22 This equation is rather involved and the details are not important here. However, this equation is second order and so the solutions are parameterized by two integration constants. One of these constants is fixed by the angle $\theta_{\textrm{\tiny CFT}}$ on the asymptotic boundary (i.e., the position of the entangling surface $\Sigma_{\textrm{\tiny CFT}}$ in the boundary theory), and the other, by the radius ${\tilde{r}}_{\textrm{\tiny B}}$ at which the RT surface intersects the brane, i.e., ${\tilde{r}}(z=z_{\textrm{\tiny B}})={\tilde{r}}_{\textrm{\tiny B}}$ . We are thus left with the question of fixing the boundary condition at the brane.

There are two contributions that come into play at the brane. The first is the DGP contribution in eq. (68),

$$ S_{\textrm{\tiny brane}}=\frac{L^{d-2}\,\Omega_{d-2}}{4\,G_{\textrm{\tiny brane}}}\,\left[\frac{L}{z_{\textrm{\tiny B}}}\left(1+\frac{z_{\textrm{\tiny B}}^{2}}{4\,L^{2}}\right)\sinh{\tilde{r}}_{\textrm{\tiny B}}\right]^{d-2}\,. $$

The second is a boundary term that comes from integrating by parts in the variation of the RT functional (75). Combining these, one arrives at the following expression2323 23 Implicitly, we assume that we care considering the RT surfaces with a cylindrical topology, i.e., in the connected phase. Examining these boundary terms carefully, one also finds that they are eliminated with ${\tilde{r}}_{\textrm{\tiny B}}=0$ . This solution points towards the existence of the second phase of disconnected surfaces, which do not intersect the brane.

$$ L\,\frac{d{\tilde{r}}}{dz}\bigg|_{z=z_{\textrm{\tiny B}}}=\frac{1}{G_{\textrm{\tiny brane}}}\,\frac{z_{\textrm{\tiny B}}/L}{1+\frac{z_{\textrm{\tiny B}}^{2}}{4\,L^{2}}}\left[\left(1+\frac{z_{\textrm{\tiny B}}^{2}}{4\,L^{2}}\right)^{2}\left(\frac{2L}{G_{\textrm{\tiny bulk}}}\,\tanh{\tilde{r}}_{\textrm{\tiny B}}\right)^{2}-\left(\frac{z_{\textrm{\tiny B}}/L}{G_{\textrm{\tiny brane}}}\right)^{2}\right]^{-\frac{1}{2}}\,. $$

Hence, scanning through the family of RT surfaces parametrized by ${\tilde{r}}_{\textrm{\tiny B}}$ , the solution which satisfies the above boundary condition is the one that properly extremizes the full entropy functional in eq. (68). One observation is that without the DGP term, i.e., $1/G_{\textrm{\tiny brane}}=0$ , the boundary condition simplifies to $L\,{d{\tilde{r}}}/{dz}|_{z=z_{\textrm{\tiny B}}}=0$ . That is, the RT surface intersects the brane at a right angle. Turning on the gravitational action on the brane (with a positive coupling) produces $L\,{d{\tilde{r}}}/{dz}|_{z=z_{\textrm{\tiny B}}}>0$ , which arises from pushing ${\tilde{r}}_{\textrm{\tiny B}}$ to a smaller value. The decrease in ${\tilde{r}}_{\textrm{\tiny B}}$ is natural here because the DGP contribution in eq. (76) adds an additional penalty for large areas on the brane and the effect is to shrink the area of $\sigma_{\mathbf{R}}$ .2424 24 If $1/G_{\textrm{\tiny brane}}<0$ as we consider in section 4.4, then the DGP entropy (76) facilitates a larger area for $\sigma_{\mathbf{R}}$ and so we find that ${\tilde{r}}_{\textrm{\tiny B}}$ increases. This is illustrated in the left panel of figure 6.

We observe that the above analysis has a simple interpretation in terms of the island rule (69). Recall that extremizing the RT functional (75) leads to a family of bulk solutions that are parametrized by ${\tilde{r}}_{\textrm{\tiny B}}$ , their radius on the brane. Evaluating $S_{\textrm{\tiny bulk}}+S_{\textrm{\tiny brane}}$ for these different solutions is equivalent to evaluating the $S_{\textrm{\tiny gen}}$ in eq. (69) with different candidates for the island geometry. The final step of extremizing with respect to variations of ${\tilde{r}}_{\textrm{\tiny B}}$ then matches the extremization in the island rule and identifies the quantum extremal surface $\sigma_{\mathbf{R}}$ on the brane.

Next, we provide a more general geometric discussion of the boundary conditions. The orthogonality between the RT surface and the RS brane is a special feature of the reflection symmetry of our setup. For a better geometric understanding of the boundary conditions, let us examine eq. (68) in more detail. Consider a $(d-1)$ -dimensional surface $\mathbf{V}$ parametrized by intrinsic coordinates $\xi^{\alpha}$ , embedded in the $(d+1)$ -dimensional bulk spacetime with coordinates $X^{\mu}$ and metric $g_{\mu\nu}$ . Hence we describe the embedding of this surface in the bulk spacetime as $X^{\mu}=X^{\mu}(\xi^{\alpha})$ , and the induced metric then becomes

$$ h_{\alpha\beta}=g_{\mu\nu}\,\frac{\partial X^{\mu}}{\partial\xi^{\alpha}}\,\frac{\partial X^{\nu}}{\partial\xi^{\beta}}\,. $$

Hence the bulk contribution in eq. (68) becomes

$$ S_{\textrm{\tiny bulk}}=\frac{A(\mathbf{V})}{4G_{\textrm{\tiny bulk}}}=\frac{1}{4G_{\textrm{\tiny bulk}}}\int_{\mathbf{V}}d^{d-1}\xi\;\sqrt{h}\,. $$

Next to evaluate the brane contribution in eq. (68), we introduce $(d-2)$ coordinates $y^{a}$ to parameterize the intersection of $\mathbf{V}$ and the brane. The induced metric on this intersection surface then becomes

$$ {\tilde{h}}_{ab}=h_{\alpha\beta}\frac{\partial\xi^{\alpha}}{\partial y^{a}}\frac{\partial\xi^{\beta}}{\partial y^{b}}\,, $$

and the corresponding contribution to the generalized entropy is

$$ \displaystyle S_{\textrm{\tiny brane}}= \displaystyle\frac{1}{4G_{\textrm{\tiny brane}}}\int d^{d-2}y\;\sqrt{{\tilde{h}}}\,. $$

Now following the prescription in eq. (68), we wish to extremize the sum of the two quantities above. So we begin with the variation of $S_{\textrm{\tiny bulk}}$ , which yields

$$ \begin{split}\delta S_{\textrm{\tiny bulk}}=&\frac{1}{4G_{\textrm{\tiny bulk}}}\Bigg[\int_{\mathbf{V}\cap{\rm brane}}\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!d^{d-2}y\,\sqrt{{\tilde{h}}}\,g_{\mu\nu}\,(\partial_{n_{\textrm{\tiny R}}}X^{\mu}+\partial_{n_{\textrm{\tiny L}}}X^{\mu})\,\delta X^{\nu}\\
&\qquad+\int_{\mathbf{V}}d^{d-1}\xi\sqrt{h}\,[\text{e.o.m.}]_{\nu}\,\delta X^{\nu}\Bigg]\,.\end{split} $$

Here we assume that the equations of motion along the bulk of $\mathbf{V}$ can be satisfied and so the second term above vanishes. However, one must integrate by parts to arrive at these equations and so we are left with a boundary term where $\mathbf{V}$ crosses the brane.2525 25 Dirichlet boundary conditions remove the analogous boundary contributions at the asymptotic AdS boundary. Here we are assuming that the extremal surface is not necessarily smooth at the brane and so $n_{\textrm{\tiny R}}^{\alpha}$ and $n_{\textrm{\tiny L}}^{\alpha}$ are unit normals to the intersection surface directed along the extremal surface approaching the brane from either side.

In the absence of the DGP term (49), there is no brane contribution (81) and then the vanishing of the boundary term in eq. (82) dictates $n_{\textrm{\tiny R}}^{\alpha}+n_{\textrm{\tiny L}}^{\alpha}=0$ .2626 26 Actually, the requirement is ${\tilde{g}}_{i\alpha}(n_{\textrm{\tiny R}}^{\alpha}+n_{\textrm{\tiny L}}^{\alpha})=0$ , i.e., the projection into the brane of the sum of the two normals vanishes – see the discussion after eq. (84). However, the vanishing of the full vector sum follows from this restriction. That is, with $1/G_{\textrm{\tiny brane}}=0$ , the boundary condition is that the RT surface should pass smoothly through the brane — this is illustrated by the solid red RT surfaces in figure 6. In the reflection symmetric setup considered above, this can only be accomplished if the RT surface is orthogonal to the brane, i.e., both $n_{\textrm{\tiny R}}^{\alpha}$ and $n_{\textrm{\tiny L}}^{\alpha}$ are orthogonal to the brane.

Of course, with a DGP brane, we must also consider the variation of $S_{\textrm{\tiny brane}}$ in eq. (81), which yields

$$ \displaystyle\delta S_{\textrm{\tiny brane}}= \displaystyle\frac{1}{4G_{\textrm{\tiny brane}}}\int d^{d-2}y\;\sqrt{{\tilde{h}}}\,\tilde{\mathcal{K}}_{i}\,\frac{\partial x^{i}}{\partial X^{\nu}}\,\delta X^{\nu}, $$

where $\tilde{\mathcal{K}}_{i}$ denotes the trace of the extrinsic curvature of the intersection surface on the brane, as viewed from the brane geometry (with the $d$ coordinates $x^{i}$ ).2727 27 In deriving eq. (83), we used that $\tilde{\mathcal{K}}_{i}$ gives the expansion of the area element $\sqrt{{\tilde{h}}}$ under the map produced by geodesics shooting out normal to the intersection surface, ${\rm RT}\cap{\rm brane}$ . Requiring the sum of eqs. (82) and (83) to vanish then yields the boundary condition

$$ 0={\tilde{g}}_{j}{}^{\nu}\left(g_{\mu\nu}(\partial_{n_{\textrm{\tiny R}}}X^{\mu}+\partial_{n_{\textrm{\tiny L}}}X^{\mu})+\frac{G_{\textrm{\tiny bulk}}}{G_{\textrm{\tiny brane}}}\,\tilde{\mathcal{K}}_{i}\,\partial_{\nu}x^{i}\right)\,. $$

Here, we think of the induced metric on the brane as the bulk tensor ${\tilde{g}}_{\mu\nu}=g_{\mu\nu}-N_{\mu}N_{\nu}$ , where $N_{\mu}$ is the unit normal orthogonal to the brane. Then, the initial factor ${\tilde{g}}_{j}{}^{\nu}$ above projects the vector expression in the brackets on to the brane. This projection is required because $\delta X^{\nu}$ in eqs. (82) and (83) is restricted to be parallel to the brane.2828 28 In writing eq. (82), we have assumed that the same domain for the coordinates $\xi^{a}$ mapped to the portion of the RT surface on either side of the brane under both $X^{\mu}(y^{a})$ and $X^{\mu}(y^{a})+\delta X^{\mu}(y^{a})$ . Said another way, $S_{\textrm{\tiny bulk}}$ has the same integration limits in $y^{a}$ both before and after the variation. Hence the brane contribution (81) leads to a discontinuity in the first derivative of the RT surface at the brane, as was implicitly found in eq. (77) above.

### 4.3 Wald-Dong entropy

As alluded to above, one of the striking features of EE for subregions in quantum field theory is that the result is dominated by short wavelength modes in the vicinity of the entangling surface and the EE is UV divergent. Of course, the leading contribution is the famous area law term [95, 96, 97] and in higher dimensions, there are subleading UV divergences which are also determined by the geometry of the entangling surface (as well as the dimensionful couplings of the underlying theory). In the holographic context, these divergences arise because the RT surface in the bulk extends out to the asymptotic boundary and hence the unregulated area is infinite [7, 6, 9]. In the context of braneworld gravity, like the construction in the previous section with $z_{\textrm{\tiny B}}\ll L$ , one expects large UV contributions when the RT surface crosses the brane. However, in this instance, the corresponding UV cutoff remains finite and set by the position of the brane, as discussed above. We show below that the corresponding UV contributions to the holographic EE can be interpreted as the Wald-Dong entropy [98, 99, 100, 101]2929 29 Our calculations will include the subleading contributions arising from the curvature-squared terms in eq. (23). Because the corresponding quantum extremal surfaces have nonvanishing extrinsic curvature, we will need the full expression for the gravitational entropy derived by Dong [101]. of the induced gravity on the brane [63, 64]. Of course, the leading UV contributions studied here do not probe the full bulk profile of the RT surface, and we leave the full calculation of holographic EE to Section 4.4.

=\frac{z_{\textrm{\tiny B}}^{2}}{4(d-4)G_{\textrm{\tiny bulk}}L}\int d^{d-2}y\;\sqrt{{\tilde{h}}}\,, $$

which matches the $\mathcal{O}(z_{\textrm{\tiny B}}^{2}/L^{2})$ term in eq. (94). Hence, as expected [63, 64], in the regime $z_{\textrm{\tiny B}}\ll L$ , one finds that the leading contributions to the holographic entanglement entropy (68) where the RT surface crosses the brane reproduce the Wald-Dong entropy of the intersection surface derived for the gravity action (23).

To close this section, we briefly remark on the case of $d=2$ , which is somewhat special in that the intersection between the RT surface and the brane is a point. Consequently, the leading UV contribution to entropy is not a standard area term, but rather a logarithmic term. Integrating the RT area (in this case, length) across gives

$$ S\simeq\frac{L}{2G_{\textrm{\tiny bulk}}}\log\left(\frac{\ell_{\textrm{\tiny IR}}}{z_{\textrm{\tiny B}}}\right)\,. $$

where an IR length scale $\ell_{\textrm{\tiny IR}}$ must appear to make the argument of the logarithm dimensionless.3333 33 As in eq. (91), a factor of two has been included to account for both sides of the brane.

Following [103], we can find (the leading contribution to) the gravitational entropy for the brane theory evaluating the Wald entropy formula [98] to the Polyakov-Liouville action (30), and then substituting the on-shell solution (32) for the scalar $\phi$ ,3434 34 Note that the action (30) is multiplied by a factor of two for the full induced brane action, i.e., $I_{\textrm{\tiny induced}}=2\,I_{\textrm{\tiny diver}}+I_{\textrm{\tiny brane}}$ .

$$ S=\frac{L}{4G_{\textrm{\tiny bulk}}}\,\phi_{0}=-\frac{L}{4G_{\textrm{\tiny bulk}}}\,\log\!\left(-\frac{L^{2}\tilde{R}}{2}\right)\,. $$

Now substituting $\tilde{R}\simeq-2z_{\textrm{\tiny B}}^{2}/L^{4}$ reproduces the leading singular behaviour in the holographic result (97). The same answer can be obtained by evaluating the Wald-Dong entropy formula [98, 101] directly on the induced gravity action (37). Hence, once again in this special case, the holographic entanglement entropy (68) reproduces the Wald-Dong entropy for the corresponding gravity action on the brane.

### 4.4 Explicit Calculations

In this section, we explicitly evaluate the holographic EE and examine the transition between the two classes of RT surfaces. While we set up the calculations for general $d>2$ , our explicit results are given for $d=3$ in which case the bulk spacetime locally has the geometry of AdS4. We add some comments about $d=2$ , and the addition of Jackiw-Teitelboim gravity (41) on the brane, in the discussion section.

#### Setting up the calculation for general dimension

In section 4.2, we reviewed two different coordinate systems in AdSd+1. The AdSd foliation (71) was well suited to discuss the brane geometry, while the global coordinates are adapted to discuss the background geometry of the boundary CFT. However, our explicit calculations of the holographic EE are best performed in a new ‘cylindrical’ coordinate system. In particular, following [104], we introduce cylindrical coordinates $P,\,\zeta$ where $\zeta$ specifies the position along the axis of the cylinder while $P$ measure the distance from the axis. These are related to the global coordinates in eq. (72) by

$$ \displaystyle\cosh r \displaystyle=\sqrt{P^{2}+1}\,\cosh\zeta\,, \displaystyle\tan\theta \displaystyle=\frac{P}{\sqrt{1+P^{2}}}\,\frac{1}{\sinh\zeta}\,, $$

while the rest of the spherical angles remain unchanged. With this transformation, the metric becomes

$$ ds^{2}=L^{2}\left[-(P^{2}+1)\cosh^{2}\zeta\,dt^{2}+\frac{dP^{2}}{1+P^{2}}+\left(1+P^{2}\right)d\zeta^{2}+P^{2}\,d\Omega_{d-2}^{2}\right]\,. $$

The range of these coordinates is $P\in(0,\infty)$ and $\zeta\in(-\infty,\infty)$ . The conformal boundary is reached with $P\to\infty$ (or $\zeta\to\pm\infty$ with fixed $P$ ). The upper ( $0\leq\theta\leq\pi/2$ ) and lower ( $\pi/2\leq\theta\leq\pi$ ) hemispheres are mapped to the upper ( $\zeta\geq 0$ ) and lower ( $\zeta\leq 0$ ) halves of the cylindrical system. The conformal defect is positioned at $\zeta=0$ . As noted above, the RT surfaces will be restricted to a constant time surface and hence the convenience of the cylindrical coordinates becomes evident, i.e., $\zeta$ becomes an extra Killing coordinate in the corresponding spatial geometry.

A few more technical details are needed for our calculations: in cylindrical coordinates (101), the boundary entangling surface corresponds to the two circles $\zeta=\pm\zeta_{\textrm{\tiny CFT}}$ , where

$$ \sinh\zeta_{\textrm{\tiny CFT}}=\tan\theta_{\textrm{\tiny CFT}}\,, $$

seen in the limit $P\to\infty$ of the second line in eq. (99). Using the AdS foliation of eq. (71), the position of the brane was $z=z_{\textrm{\tiny B}}$ . Using eq. (74), the brane position can be specified in cylindrical coordinates (101) according to

$$ \left(1+P^{2}\right)\sinh^{2}\!\zeta=\frac{L^{2}}{z_{\textrm{\tiny B}}^{2}}\left(1-\frac{z_{\textrm{\tiny B}}^{2}}{4L^{2}}\right)^{2}\,. $$

Recall that the brane intersects the asymptotic boundary at the position of the conformal defect, i.e., at $\theta=\pi/2$ with $r\to\infty$ , which corresponds to $\zeta=0$ with $P\to\infty$ in cylindrical coordinates. Further recall that RT surface areas are UV divergent since they extend to the asymptotic boundaries. Hence we introduced a UV regulator surface at $r=r_{\textrm{\tiny UV}}$ , which in cylindrical coordinates becomes

$$ (P^{2}+\tanh^{2}\zeta)\cosh^{2}\zeta=\sinh^{2}\!r_{\textrm{\tiny UV}}\,. $$

We will be mainly interested in comparing the areas of different surfaces for fixed $\zeta_{\textrm{\tiny CFT}}$ , as discussed above. Since the UV divergent terms only depend of the geometry of the entangling surface, they will cancel in the difference of the two areas. Hence, we can then safely take the UV cutoff to infinity.

As noted, the RT surfaces all lie in a fixed time slice and thus we only need consider configurations with cylindrical symmetry (i.e., rotational symmetry on the $S^{d-2}$ ). Hence it is convenient to use the cylindrical coordinates (101) and parametrize the profile of the bulk surfaces as $\zeta=\zeta(P)$ . The bulk contribution to the holographic EE is given by

$$ \displaystyle S_{\textrm{\tiny bulk}}=\frac{L^{d-1}\,\Omega_{d-2}}{2\,G_{\textrm{\tiny bulk}}}\int dPP^{d-2}\sqrt{\frac{1}{1+P^{2}}+(1+P^{2})\,\zeta^{\prime 2}} $$

where again $\Omega_{d-2}$ is the area of the unit $(d-2)$ -sphere – see footnote 21. As in eq. (75), an overall factor of 2 is included here to account for the reflection symmetry of the profile $\zeta(P)$ about the brane. Since this expression does not contain an explicit $\zeta$ dependence, it is straightforward to derive

$$ \displaystyle\zeta^{\prime}(P)=\pm\frac{1}{1+P^{2}}\,\sqrt{\frac{P_{0}^{2(d-2)}\left(1+P_{0}^{2}\right)}{P^{2(d-2)}\left(1+P^{2}\right)-P_{0}^{2(d-2)}\left(1+P_{0}^{2}\right)}} $$

where the two branches correspond to two identical surfaces related by a reflection with respect to $\zeta=0$ . $P_{0}$ corresponds to the turning point, where the surface makes its closest approach to the symmetry axis.

We now discuss the disconnected phase described at the beginning of this section. It corresponds to the ‘trivial’ solution with $P_{0}=0$ . We find $\zeta(P)=\pm\zeta_{\textrm{\tiny CFT}}$ , which in cylindrical coordinates looks simply as a pair of disks anchored at the boundary entangling surface. Substituting $\zeta^{\prime}=0$ into eq. (105), the area of the two discs can be integrated up to some cutoff radius $P_{\textrm{\tiny UV}}$ , and the corresponding holographic EE is

$$ \displaystyle S_{\textrm{\tiny disc}}=\frac{L^{d-1}\,\Omega_{d-2}}{2(d-1)\,G_{\textrm{\tiny bulk}}}\ P_{\textrm{\tiny UV}}^{d-1}\,{}_{2}F_{1}\left[\frac{1}{2},\frac{d-1}{2},\frac{d+1}{2},-P_{\textrm{\tiny UV}}^{2}\right]\,. $$

In this case, the entanglement wedge corresponds to two identical disconnected pieces contained between each component of the RT surface and the asymptotic boundary, i.e., the regions $\zeta\geq+\zeta_{\textrm{\tiny CFT}}$ and $\zeta\leq-\zeta_{\textrm{\tiny CFT}}$ , as sketched in the upper panel of figure 8.

*Figure 8: Sketch of fixed time slices of our symmetric setup, showing the two possible configurations. The shaded red region corresponds to the entanglement wedge. The connected solution contains an island on the brane, where gravity is dynamical.*

The connected phase corresponds to $P_{0}>0$ , which leads to a cylindrical RT surface. Integrating eq. (106) yields a family of bulk surfaces, which are symmetric about the brane and which are anchored on the asymptotic boundary at $\zeta=\pm\zeta_{\textrm{\tiny CFT}}$ . Recalling the discussion below eq. (75), we observe that in this configuration, $P_{0}$ is the second integration constant which must be tuned in order to satisfy the appropriate boundary condition (77) at the brane, see the lower panel of figure 8.

Before we calculate the entropy in the most general setting, let us consider the case of a zero-tension brane with $1/G_{\textrm{\tiny brane}}=0$ , i.e., empty AdSd+1. In this case, the brane is positioned at $z_{\textrm{\tiny B}}=2L$ or simply, $\zeta=0$ . Now, the ‘plus’ branch of eq. (106) can be integrated to produce a profile extending from $P=P_{\textrm{\tiny UV}}$ at $\zeta=+\zeta_{\textrm{\tiny CFT}}$ to the maximal depth $P=P_{0}$ at some $\zeta=\zeta_{0}(\zeta_{\textrm{\tiny CFT}},P_{0})<\zeta_{\textrm{\tiny CFT}}$ . Since eq. (77) indicates that the RT surface must intersect the brane orthogonally, we must tune $P_{0}$ (with fixed $\zeta_{\textrm{\tiny CFT}}$ ) such that $\zeta_{0}=0$ , i.e., the RT surface reaches its maximal depth at the brane position. Now, substituting eq. (106) into eq. (105), the holographic EE (for empty AdSd+1) becomes

$$ \displaystyle S_{\textrm{\tiny conn}}(T_{o}=0) \displaystyle=\frac{L^{d-1}\,\Omega_{d-2}}{2\,G_{\textrm{\tiny bulk}}}\int_{P_{0}}^{P_{\textrm{\tiny UV}}}\!\!\!dP\,\frac{P^{2(d-2)}}{\sqrt{P^{2(d-2)}(1+P^{2})-P_{0}^{2(d-2)}(1+P_{0}^{2})}}\,. $$

In the general case, this exercise is slightly more complicated for the case of interest with a finite-tension DGP brane at some $z=z_{\textrm{\tiny B}}\ll L$ , and the geometry of the corresponding RT surface is illustrated in the lower panel of figure 8. The RT surface is again symmetric about the brane and so as above, we focus on the portion starting at $\zeta=+\zeta_{\textrm{\tiny CFT}}$ at the asymptotic boundary (i.e., at $P=P_{\textrm{\tiny UV}}$ ). As before, the ‘plus’ branch of eq. (106) produces a surface reaching its maximal depth $P=P_{0}$ at some $\zeta=\zeta_{0}(\zeta_{\textrm{\tiny CFT}},P_{0})<\zeta_{\textrm{\tiny CFT}}$ .3535 35 In fact, $\zeta_{0}(\zeta_{\textrm{\tiny CFT}},P_{0})$ is precisely the same function introduced above, since the turning point of the RT surfaces are completely independent of the brane properties. Now one continues from this point using the ‘minus’ branch of eq. (106), which then meets the brane as some $P=P_{\textrm{\tiny B}}(\zeta_{\textrm{\tiny CFT}},P_{0})$ and $\zeta=\zeta_{\textrm{\tiny B}}(\zeta_{\textrm{\tiny CFT}},P_{0})$ .3636 36 Of course, $P_{\textrm{\tiny B}}$ and $\zeta_{\textrm{\tiny B}}$ are related as in eq. (103). One would again tune $P_{0}$ (for fixed $\zeta_{\textrm{\tiny CFT}}$ ) to ensure the appropriate boundary condition (77) is satisfied at the brane. The bulk contribution to the holographic EE then becomes

$$ \displaystyle S_{\textrm{\tiny conn}}(T_{o}>0) \displaystyle= \displaystyle\frac{L^{d-1}\,\Omega_{d-2}}{2\,G_{\textrm{\tiny bulk}}}\left[\int_{P_{0}}^{P_{\textrm{\tiny UV}}}\!\!\!dP\,\frac{P^{2(d-2)}}{\sqrt{P^{2(d-2)}(1+P^{2})-P_{0}^{2(d-2)}(1+P_{0}^{2})}}\right. \displaystyle\qquad\qquad\qquad+\left.\int_{P_{0}}^{P_{\textrm{\tiny B}}}\!\!dP\,\frac{P^{2(d-2)}}{\sqrt{P^{2(d-2)}(1+P^{2})-P_{0}^{2(d-2)}(1+P_{0}^{2})}}\right]\,. $$

Of course, if there is no gravitational term on the brane (e.g., as in eq. (49)), then this expression yields the entire generalized entropy (1) for the connected phase. Now rather than explicitly examining the brane boundary condition (77) in cylindrical coordinates, we will simply evaluate the generalized entropy and find the minimum numerically in the following. Hence to proceed further we will have to choose a specific value for the boundary dimension $d$ .

#### Explicit results for $d=3$

In this section, we consider the above discussion for $d=3$ , in which case the boundary geometry becomes $\mathbb{R}\times S^{2}$ , the bulk spacetime is locally AdS4, and the branes have an AdS3 geometry. We will also consider supplementing the the four-dimensional bulk action (4) with a Gauss-Bonnet term,

$$ I_{\textrm{\tiny top}}=\frac{\lambda_{\textrm{\tiny GB}}}{16\pi^{2}}\int\mathrm{d}^{4}x\,\sqrt{-g}\,\left[R_{abcd}R^{abcd}-4\,R_{ab}R^{ab}+R^{2}\right]\,. $$

Note that we have ignored the necessary boundary terms which ensure that this interaction is proportional to the Euler density, e.g., see [105]. Although this curvature-squared term does not effect the bulk equations of motion, it will contribute to the generalized entropy [101, 106]3737 37 One may worry that the topological nature of $I_{\textrm{\tiny top}}$ undercuts the usual derivations of the generalized entropy. However, individually the three terms in eq. (110) are dynamical and one can apply the results of [101] for each separately and then take the sum of the corresponding contributions to the holographic entropy, which one finds matches the result in eq. (111).

$$ S_{\textrm{\tiny JM}}=\frac{\lambda_{\textrm{\tiny GB}}}{4\pi}\int_{\Sigma_{\mathbf{R}}}d^{2}x\sqrt{h}\,{\cal R}+\frac{\lambda_{\textrm{\tiny GB}}}{2\pi}\int_{\partial\Sigma_{\mathbf{R}}}dx\sqrt{h}\,{\cal K}_{g}\,, $$

where ${\cal R}$ denotes the Ricci scalar for the intrinsic geometry on the RT surface $\Sigma_{\mathbf{R}}$ . Similarly, ${\cal K}_{g}$ denotes the geodesic curvature of the boundary $\partial\Sigma_{\mathbf{R}}$ . Of course, eq. (111) gives a topological contribution proportional to the Euler character of the two-dimensional extremal surfaces3838 38 The normalization is chosen so that for an RT surface with two-sphere topology, $S_{\textrm{\tiny JM}}=2\lambda_{\textrm{\tiny GB}}$ . and so their geometry remains unaffected by this term. However, in the following, this additional contribution will provide an extra parameter which allows us to adjust the transition between the connected and disconnected phases.

For $d=3$ , some analytic expressions for the extremal surfaces can be obtained [104]. For example, integrating eq. (106) yields the following profile for the extremal surface in empty AdS4 [104]

$$ \displaystyle\zeta_{\pm}(P;P_{0},\zeta_{0})=\zeta_{0}\pm\frac{P_{0}}{\sqrt{(1+P_{0}^{2})(1+2P_{0}^{2})}} \displaystyle\times\left[(1+P_{0}^{2})\,F\!\left(\mbox{Arcos}\frac{P_{0}}{P},\sqrt{\frac{1+P_{0}^{2}}{1+2P_{0}^{2}}}\right)-P_{0}^{2}\,\Pi\!\left(\mbox{Arccos}\frac{P_{0}}{P},\frac{1}{1+P_{0}^{2}},\sqrt{\frac{1+P_{0}^{2}}{1+2P_{0}^{2}}}\right)\right] $$

where $F$ and $\Pi$ correspond to incomplete elliptic integrals of the first and third kind, respectively.3939 39 Our notation for the elliptic integrals matches that in [107], section 8.1. Again, the $\pm$ branches correspond to the two portions of the surface, symmetric with respect to $\zeta_{0}=0$ . Of course, we need to know where this surface is anchored at the boundary. Hence we define

$$ \displaystyle\zeta_{\infty} \displaystyle\equiv \displaystyle\zeta_{+}(P\to\infty;P_{0},\zeta_{0})-\zeta_{0} \displaystyle= \displaystyle\frac{P_{0}\left[(1+P_{0}^{2})\,K\!\left(\sqrt{\frac{1+P_{0}^{2}}{1+2P_{0}^{2}}}\right)-P_{0}^{2}\,\Pi\!\left(\frac{1}{1+P_{0}^{2}},\sqrt{\frac{1+P_{0}^{2}}{1+2P_{0}^{2}}}\right)\right]}{\sqrt{(1+P_{0}^{2})(1+2P_{0}^{2})}} $$

and the surface reaches the asymptotic boundary at $\zeta_{\pm}(P\to\infty)=\zeta_{0}\pm\zeta_{\infty}$ . Hence the two components of the entangling surface in the boundary theory are separated by $2\zeta_{\infty}$ , in the cylindrical coordinates.

Figure 9 plots $\zeta_{\infty}$ as a function of $P_{0}$ . The maximum is obtained at $P_{0}=P_{0}^{\textrm{\tiny crit}}\approx 0.51633$ with $\zeta_{\infty}=\zeta_{\infty}^{\textrm{\tiny crit}}\approx 0.5011$ . An interesting observation in [104] was that, for $P_{0}<P_{0}^{\textrm{\tiny crit}}$ , there exist two values of $P_{0}$ with the same $\zeta_{\infty}$ . That is, if the two components of the entangling surface are sufficiently ‘close’ on the boundary sphere, there actually exist two extremal RT surfaces that connect them in the bulk. However, one branch (with the smaller value of $P_{0}$ ) is always subdominant, and therefore will be of little interest in our analysis. On the other hand, if the separation of the two entangling spheres is larger than the critical value $2\zeta_{\infty}^{\text{max}}$ (in cylindrical coordinates), there is no connected extremal surface that joins them.

*Figure 9: Plot of the ‘height’ of the RT surface in cylindrical coordinates, as a function of the turning point $P_{0}$ characterising the surface. For $\zeta_{\infty}<\zeta_{\infty}^{\textrm{\tiny crit}}$ , there are two minimal surfaces anchored at the same regions; otherwise there exists none.*

Let us now describe the solutions corresponding to different values of the tension and DGP term:

#### a) $T_{o}=0;\ 1/G_{\textrm{\tiny brane}}=0$ :

First we consider the holographic EE in empty AdS4 as a lead-in to the case with a brane. As emphasized above, the area of these surfaces is divergent, and so one introduces a UV regulator surface, integrating of the area from $P_{0}$ to some $P_{\textrm{\tiny UV}}\gg 1$ [104]. For the disconnected solution (i.e., a pair of disks), eq. (107) with $d=3$ gives

$$ \displaystyle S_{\textrm{\tiny disc}}(P_{\textrm{\tiny UV}})= \displaystyle\frac{\pi L^{2}}{G_{\textrm{\tiny bulk}}}\,\left(\sqrt{1+P_{\textrm{\tiny UV}}^{2}}-1\right)+2\lambda_{\textrm{\tiny GB}} \displaystyle= \displaystyle\frac{A(S^{1}_{P_{\textrm{\tiny UV}}})}{4G_{\textrm{\tiny eff}}}-\frac{\pi L^{2}}{G_{\textrm{\tiny bulk}}}+2\lambda_{\textrm{\tiny GB}}+\mathcal{O}(P_{\textrm{\tiny UV}}^{-1})\,. $$

where

$$ \frac{A(S^{1}_{P})}{4G_{\textrm{\tiny eff}}}=\frac{\pi L^{2}}{G_{\textrm{\tiny bulk}}}\,P\,, $$

is the length of $S^{1}_{P}$ , a circle with radius $P$ , and we used eq. (24) to write $\frac{1}{G_{\textrm{\tiny eff}}}=\frac{2\,L}{G_{\textrm{\tiny bulk}}}$ . We have included in eq. (114) the topological contribution in eq. (111). On the other hand, for the connected surfaces the area formula (108) yields

$$ \displaystyle\begin{split}&S_{\textrm{\tiny conn}}(P_{\textrm{\tiny UV}},P_{0})\\
=&\frac{\pi L^{2}}{G_{\textrm{\tiny bulk}}}\,\frac{P_{0}^{2}}{\sqrt{1+2P_{0}^{2}}}\,\Pi\!\left(\mbox{Arccos}\frac{P_{0}}{P_{\textrm{\tiny UV}}},1,\sqrt{\frac{1+P_{0}^{2}}{1+2P_{0}^{2}}}\right)\end{split} \displaystyle\begin{split}=&\frac{A(S^{1}_{P_{\textrm{\tiny UV}}})}{4G_{\textrm{\tiny eff}}}+\frac{\pi L^{2}}{G_{\textrm{\tiny bulk}}}\left[-\sqrt{1+2P_{0}^{2}}E\left(\sqrt{\frac{1+P_{0}^{2}}{1+2P_{0}^{2}}}\right)+\frac{P_{0}^{2}}{\sqrt{1+2P_{0}^{2}}}K\left(\sqrt{\frac{1+P_{0}^{2}}{1+2P_{0}^{2}}}\right)\right]\\
&+\mathcal{O}(P_{\textrm{\tiny UV}}^{-1})\,,\end{split} $$

where $E$ is the elliptic integral of the second kind. We emphasize that this result only applies for vanishing $T_{o}$ and vanishing $1/G_{\textrm{\tiny brane}}$ , i.e., for the AdS4 vacuum. Note that the Euler character of the cylindrical RT surface is zero and hence there is no contribution proportional to $\lambda_{\textrm{\tiny GB}}$ . As expected, the divergence in the $P_{\textrm{\tiny UV}}\to\infty$ limit matches for the areas of the connected and disconnected surfaces. Hence we can safely take the limit when considering the difference

$$ \displaystyle\Delta S(P_{0}) \displaystyle=\lim_{P_{\textrm{\tiny UV}}\to\infty}\left(S_{\textrm{\tiny conn}}(P_{\textrm{\tiny UV}},P_{0})-S_{\textrm{\tiny disc}}(P_{\textrm{\tiny UV}})\right)\,, $$

given by the difference in $O\left(\left(P_{0}/P_{\textrm{\tiny UV}}\right)^{0}\right)$ terms in eq. (118) and eq. (115). A plot of $\Delta S$ is shown in figure 10. When $\Delta S>0$ , the disconnected RT surface is the dominant saddle, while for $\Delta S<0$ , the connected solution dominates. Notice that with a larger (positive) topolgical coupling $\lambda_{\textrm{\tiny GB}}$ , the entropy in eq. (114) increases while eq. (117) is unaffected, and hence the range of the disconnected phase is decreased in figure 10.

*Figure 10: Renormalised entropy from eq. (119). The connected (disconnected) surface dominates when $\Delta S<0\,(\Delta S>0)$ . When $\lambda_{\textrm{\tiny GB}}$ becomes very large, $\lambda_{\textrm{\tiny GB}}\sim c_{T}$ , the connected solution becomes favoured.*

#### b) $T_{o}\neq 0;\ 1/G_{\textrm{\tiny brane}}=0$ :

The next step is to introduce the brane, however, we do not include a gravitational term in the brane action yet, i.e., $1/G_{\textrm{\tiny brane}}=0$ . In this case, we saw in eq. (109) that there is an additional contribution as the RT surface extends from the maximal depth $P_{0}$ back out to meet the brane at $P_{\textrm{\tiny B}}$ . Both contributions in eq. (109) take the same form except for the limits of integration, hence the $d=3$ result in eq. (117) is replaced by

$$ \displaystyle S_{\textrm{\tiny conn}}(P_{\textrm{\tiny UV}},P_{0}) \displaystyle= \displaystyle\frac{\pi L^{2}}{G_{\textrm{\tiny bulk}}}\,\frac{P_{0}^{2}}{\sqrt{1+2P_{0}^{2}}}\,\left[\Pi\!\left(\mbox{Arccos}\frac{P_{0}}{P_{\textrm{\tiny UV}}},1,\sqrt{\frac{1+P_{0}^{2}}{1+2P_{0}^{2}}}\right)\right. \displaystyle\left.\qquad\qquad+\Pi\!\left(\mbox{Arccos}\frac{P_{0}}{P_{\textrm{\tiny B}}},1,\sqrt{\frac{1+P_{0}^{2}}{1+2P_{0}^{2}}}\right)\right]\,. $$

Of course, the entropy for the disconnected phase remains the same as in eq. (114) and we can consider the difference of the generalized entropy evaluated on the connected and disconnected extremal surfaces, as in eq. (119). Just as we saw a leading divergent contribution in eq. (117) for $P_{\textrm{\tiny UV}}\to\infty$ , we expect that eq. (120) will contain an analogous large contribution for $P_{\textrm{\tiny B}}\gg P_{0}$ . However, this term will not be cancelled in $\Delta S$ . In fact, in this regime, we can expand the difference as

$$ \displaystyle\begin{split}&\Delta S(P_{0})\\
=&\frac{A(\sigma_{\mathbf{R}})}{4G_{\textrm{\tiny eff}}}+\frac{\pi L^{2}}{G_{\textrm{\tiny bulk}}}\left[1-2\sqrt{1+2P_{0}^{2}}E\left(\sqrt{\frac{1+P_{0}^{2}}{1+2P_{0}^{2}}}\right)+\frac{2P_{0}^{2}}{\sqrt{1+2P_{0}^{2}}}K\left(\sqrt{\frac{1+P_{0}^{2}}{1+2P_{0}^{2}}}\right)\right]\\
&-2\lambda_{\textrm{\tiny GB}}+\mathcal{O}(P_{\textrm{\tiny B}}^{-1})\,.\end{split} $$

Here, the intersection $\sigma_{\mathbf{R}}$ of the RT surface and the brane is a circle of radius $P_{\textrm{\tiny B}}$ with area $A(\sigma_{\mathbf{R}})=2\pi L\,P_{\textrm{\tiny B}}$ given by eq. (101). The fact that the leading term can be expressed as the gravitational entropy for the induced gravity action (23) on the brane is in perfect agreement with our discussion in the previous section. As we will see below, the finite terms will play a role once we turn on the DGP term, allowing for the appearance of a different island on the brane.

From the above expansion, we see that there is a strong penalty for having a large $\sigma_{\mathbf{R}}$ in the connected phase. From the brane perspective, the gravitational entropy results in a large penalty against forming an island on the brane. In fact, generally we expect that $\Delta S>0$ in this regime and hence the disconnected solution provides the dominant saddle point. However, if we tune the topological coupling $\lambda_{\textrm{\tiny GB}}$ to be large4040 40 We note that this requires $\lambda_{\textrm{\tiny GB}}\sim{L^{2}}/{G_{\textrm{\tiny bulk}}}\sim c_{\textrm{\tiny T}}$ , the central charge of the boundary CFT – see further discussion in section (5). (and positive), this contribution can compensate for the leading gravitational entropy term, at least for $\sigma_{\mathbf{R}}$ up to a certain size.

On the other hand, we must note that $P_{\textrm{\tiny B}}$ is not an independent parameter. Rather it is implicitly determined by $\zeta_{\textrm{\tiny CFT}}$ and the brane tension $T_{o}$ , as well as the value of $P_{0}$ that minimises the area functional in eq. (121). $P_{\textrm{\tiny B}}$ can be determined in the following way (see figure 8). One begins by solving for $\zeta_{0}$ using $\zeta_{0}+\zeta_{\infty}(P_{0})=\zeta_{\textrm{\tiny CFT}}$ where $\zeta_{\infty}(P_{0})$ is given in eq. (113). Then one finds ‘sample’ values of $P_{\textrm{\tiny B}},\zeta_{\textrm{\tiny B}}$ where the extremal surface meets the brane by combining eqs. (103) and (112) and simultaneously solving

$$ \displaystyle\left(1+P_{\textrm{\tiny B}}^{2}\right)\sinh^{2}\!\zeta_{\textrm{\tiny B}} \displaystyle= \displaystyle\frac{L^{2}}{z_{\textrm{\tiny B}}^{2}}\left(1-\frac{z_{\textrm{\tiny B}}^{2}}{4L^{2}}\right)^{2}\,, \displaystyle\zeta_{-}(P_{\textrm{\tiny B}};P_{0},\zeta_{0}) \displaystyle= \displaystyle\zeta_{\textrm{\tiny B}}\,. $$

This yields $P_{B}$ as a function of $P_{0},\zeta_{\textrm{\tiny CFT}}$ and $T_{o}$ , and substituting $P_{\textrm{\tiny B}}$ into eq. (120) gives the area of the associated extremal surface. Below, we perform this calculation numerically. However, we have not yet considered the boundary conditions (77) in this analysis. Rather than explicitly examining the latter, we simply evaluate the area (or rather the difference $\Delta S$ ) over the range of possible $P_{0}$ (with fixed $\zeta_{\textrm{\tiny CFT}},T_{o}$ ), as shown in figure 11a. The correct RT surfaces are then identified as the minima in these plots. Further, the examples in the figure illustrate that without the topological contribution, $\Delta S>0$ for all minima and so the disconnected phase dominates, as generally expected. That is, no quantum extremal islands form on the brane in this case. However, as shown in figure 11b, we see that with a sufficiently large topological coupling $\lambda_{\textrm{\tiny GB}}$ one can achieve $\Delta S<0$ , where a first order transition leads to the formation of an island.

Although the above recipe is valid for arbitrary brane tensions, in the limit of very large tension we can approximate the solution analytically. Since, as stated above, the leading contribution to the entropy (116) scales as $A(\sigma_{\mathbf{R}})\sim P_{\textrm{\tiny B}}$ , the RT surface corresponds to that which has the minimal value of $P_{\textrm{\tiny B}}$ . Moreover, since the function $\zeta_{\textrm{\tiny B}}(P)$ defining embedding of the brane in (122) is monotonically decreasing with $P$ , the surface must maximise its hight $\zeta_{\infty}(P_{0})$ , which is achieved for $P_{0}=P_{0}^{\textrm{\tiny crit}}$ , by definition (see discussion around figure 9). This can be readily checked in figure 11a, where the curves attain a minimum around $\mbox{arctan}(P_{0}^{\textrm{\tiny crit}})\approx 0.47$ , with a small correction due to the finite terms in (121), which becomes smaller and smaller as we increase the tension. We shall refer to this solution with $P_{0}\approx P_{0}^{\textrm{\tiny crit}}$ as the small island, in order to distinguish it from a second island appearing below which corresponds to a circle with a larger radius.

*Figure 11: Panel a. illustrates the renormalised area from eq. (121) of connected RT surfaces, anchored at $\zeta_{\textrm{\tiny CFT}}=0$ , with $\lambda_{\textrm{\tiny GB}}=0$ . Panel b. is a plot of the critical value of $\lambda_{\textrm{\tiny GB}}$ such that $\mbox{min}(\Delta S)<0$ .*

#### c) $T_{o}\neq 0;\ 1/G_{\textrm{\tiny brane}}\neq 0$ :

Finally, we examine the holographic EE in the presence of a DGP brane. The only difference in this analysis is the additional contribution coming at the intersection of the RT surface with the brane in eq. (68). In the present setting, this means that we add the following,

$$ S_{\textrm{\tiny brane}}=\frac{A(\sigma_{\mathbf{R}})}{4G_{\textrm{\tiny brane}}}=\frac{\pi L}{2G_{\textrm{\tiny brane}}}\,P_{\textrm{\tiny B}}\,, $$

to the bulk contribution in eq. (120). In fact, the expansion of $\Delta S$ for $P_{\textrm{\tiny B}}\gg P_{0}$ takes precisely the same form as in eq. (121). The only difference is that the induced Newton’s constant on the brane is now given by eq. (52), i.e., $\frac{1}{G_{\textrm{\tiny eff}}}=\frac{2\,L}{G_{\textrm{\tiny bulk}}}+\frac{1}{G_{\textrm{\tiny brane}}}$ .

Generally, we might think of $1/G_{\textrm{\tiny brane}}$ as a positive quantity, and so the DGP contribution (123) would simply increase the penalty for having a large $\sigma_{\mathbf{R}}$ in the connected phase, and enhance the dominance of the disconnected phase. However, there is no apriori reason why we should not also consider a negative gravitational coupling on the brane,4141 41 For example, integrating out quantum fields on the brane could produce either a positive or negative shift in Newton’s constant. In particular, it can be negative for gauge fields or nonminimally coupled scalar fields, as discussed in the context of EE in [108, 109] – see further discussion in section 5 and appendix B. in which case the DGP term serves as another mechanism to reduce the penalty for forming an island on the brane. It is this scenario that we will examine further here – as well as in appendix B.

It will prove convenient to work with the ratio $\lambda_{b}$ introduced in eq. (53). Let us recall what parameters are in play. The tension of the brane is controlled by $z_{\textrm{\tiny B}}$ , which we keep small but finite. The dimensionless ratio between the bulk and brane gravitational constants is controlled by $\lambda_{b}$ . As discussed above, interesting things happen when $\lambda_{b}<0$ , which is when $G_{\textrm{\tiny brane}}<0$ while $G_{\textrm{\tiny bulk}}>0$ .

Using the same approach described above, we can explore the transition between the connected and disconnected phases numerically. In figure 12a, we plot $\Delta S$ as function of $P_{0}$ for a fixed $\zeta_{\textrm{\tiny CFT}}=0.095,L/z_{\textrm{\tiny B}}=100$ and $\lambda_{\textrm{\tiny GB}}=0$ , for different values of $\lambda_{b}$ . These plots are analogous to those presented in figure 12a where $\lambda_{b}=0$ (but $L/z_{\textrm{\tiny B}}$ is varied). Again, these plots are made in lieu of a detailed examination of the boundary conditions where the RT surfaces meet the brane, rather the correct boundary conditions (77) will be achieved where $P_{0}$ is tuned to produced an minimum in these plots. For small $\lambda_{b}$ the curves show a single minimum but $\Delta S>0$ , indicating that the disconnected solution dominates in this case. As $\lambda_{b}$ becomes more negative, the curves are pulled down and eventually $\Delta S$ enters the negative region so that the connected solution becomes the dominant saddle point. This behaviour is as expected but we note that $\lambda_{b}$ is very close to $-1$ in this regime, which according to eq. (53) means there is almost a complete cancelation between the induced gravitation coupling $1/G_{\textrm{\tiny RS}}$ and the DGP term $1/G_{\textrm{\tiny brane}}$ . Of course, this near cancellation is alleviated by turning on the topological coupling $\lambda_{\textrm{\tiny GB}}$ , as shown in figure 12b.

Another interesting feature shown in figure 12a is the appearance of a second minimum in the curves. This second solution occurs at a larger value of $P_{0}$ and also of $P_{B}$ , and corresponds to a larger circle $\sigma_{\mathbf{R}}$ on the brane, and therefore we refer to it as a large island. The existence of this second island is due to the finite terms in (121). Indeed, these terms are essentially what is plotted in figure 10, and they are unbounded from below for large $P_{0}$ . Therefore, when $\lambda_{b}$ becomes sufficiently negative as to produce a significant cancellation between the induced and DGP gravitational entropies, there is a new competition, now between $A(\sigma_{\mathbf{R}})/4G_{\textrm{\tiny eff}}$ and the finite terms, producing the large island. As $\lambda_{b}\to-1$ , the minimum rolls down to infinity ( $P\to\infty,\Delta S_{\textrm{\tiny gen}}\to-\infty$ ), indicating an instability at this point, which we explore further in appendix B.
